name: Sumerians
place: the marshes and river plains of southern Mesopotamia
desc: The people of Eridu, Uruk and Ur, who dug canals between the Tigris and Euphrates, built the first cities, and pressed the first writing into clay.
source: Excavations at Uruk (from 1912), Ur (Leonard Woolley, 1922–34) and Eridu; Sumerian literature from Nippur

cautious: cleared the silt from the great canal before the flood season
devout: climbed the steps of the temple terrace to watch the new moon
gluttonous: brewed a beer so good the whole village sang to Ninkasi

inventions.name: Counting Tokens
inventions.source: Small clay tokens for counting goods appear across the Near East from about 8000 BCE; at Uruk they were sealed in clay envelopes
inventions.desc: Little clay shapes, one for each jar of oil or sheep: the tribe gathers a little more lore, and the stores hold 10 more food.
inventions.hint: Comes from leading others, and evenings of keeping count.

inventions.name: Cylinder Seal
inventions.source: Carved stone cylinders rolled across wet clay, from the Uruk period (c. 3500 BCE) on
inventions.desc: A carved stone rolled over the clay that seals a jar: no one opens it unseen, and food spoils 10% slower.
inventions.hint: Needs Polished Stone Tools, and carvers who keep the rites.

inventions.name: Potter's Wheel
inventions.source: Slow wheels for turning pots were in use in Mesopotamia by about 4500–3500 BCE
inventions.desc: A heavy disc turned by hand while the potter shapes the clay: the stores hold 20 more food, and building is 5% faster.
inventions.hint: Needs pottery, and many evenings at the clay.

inventions.name: Irrigation Canals
inventions.source: Canals from the Euphrates fed the fields of Eridu and Uruk; keeping them clear was the first public work
inventions.desc: Ditches that lead the river to the fields: farm plots yield 30% more.
inventions.hint: Needs farming, and builders who work the fields.

foods.name: Barley Beer
foods.source: The Hymn to Ninkasi (c. 1800 BCE) is both a prayer and a brewing recipe; workers at Uruk were paid in beer
foods.desc: Barley bread soaked and left to work in a jar, drunk through reed straws: +4 mood, and hunger grows 5% slower.
foods.hint: Needs pottery and farming, and grain left by the fire.

foods.name: Date Cakes
foods.source: The date palm was grown in southern Mesopotamia from at least the 4th millennium BCE
foods.desc: Dates pressed into cakes that keep for a year: food spoils 15% slower.

finds.name: Date Palms
finds.desc: Tall palms heavy with sweet dates along the water.

finds.name: Reed Beds
finds.source: Marsh Arabs still build arched reed houses (mudhif) like those shown on Uruk seals
finds.desc: Tall marsh reeds, bundled for houses, boats and baskets: each load is wood.

people.name: Ninsumu
people.desc: She knows how the water must run for every field.
memory: cut the first ditch from the river to the barley field

people.name: Urengur
people.desc: He counts the barley, the sheep and the days.
memory: counted every sheep of the temple flock with clay tokens

people.name: Kubaba
people.source: Sumerian King List: the only woman listed as ruling in her own right
people.desc: A woman who kept a tavern in Kish and became its queen, said to have reigned a hundred years.

people.name: Puabi
people.source: Royal Tomb PG 800 at Ur, c. 2600 BCE
people.desc: A queen buried in a headdress of gold leaves and lapis beads, with her name rolled on a cylinder seal.

people.name: Ur-Nammu
people.source: Code of Ur-Nammu, c. 2100–2050 BCE, the oldest law code known
people.desc: The king who built the great ziggurat of Ur and wrote down laws that fined, rather than maimed, those who did wrong.

people.name: Ea-nasir
people.source: Letter of Nanni to Ea-nasir (c. 1750 BCE), British Museum: the oldest known written complaint
people.text: a merchant just back from Dilmun with copper ingots, followed by a trail of angry customers.
memory: sold copper to Nanni that Nanni swore was bad
people.desc: A copper merchant of Ur, remembered because a customer's furious letter about his poor copper survives.

people.name: Gilgamesh
people.label: Gilgamesh, Two-Thirds a God
people.desc: A king who wrestles giants. Combat 8, 85 HP.

people.name: Ziusudra
people.label: Ziusudra the Boat-Builder
people.desc: Warned by the gods, he builds the boat that outlasts the flood. Crafting 7, Lore 5.

people.name: Lugalbanda
people.label: Lugalbanda the Swift
people.desc: Given swiftness by the Anzud bird. Foraging 7, fast as the wind.

events.title: The River Changes Its Bed
events.source: The Euphrates shifted its course many times; cities like Ur and Eridu were left far from water
events.text: After the flood the river runs in a new channel, far from the fields. The old canals stand dry.

options.label: Dig a new canal to the river

do.feat: Dug a canal to the moving river

options.result: A whole season of digging. When the water flows again, the fields are greener than before.

options.label: Follow the river
options.result: The people pack up and drift toward the new water, grumbling.

events.title: Signs Pressed in Clay
events.source: Proto-cuneiform tablets from the Eanna precinct at Uruk, c. 3300–3100 BCE, are among the earliest writing
events.text: A steward tires of carrying tokens and simply presses their shapes into a flat piece of clay with a reed. The marks stay, and anyone who knows them can read the count.

do.remember: pressed the first signs into clay

events.title: The Edge of the Plain
events.source: Lagash and Umma fought for generations over the fields of the Gu-edena; the Stele of the Vultures (c. 2450 BCE) records it
events.text: Herders from a neighbouring town have moved the stone that marks where our fields end. The young men are already sharpening spears.

options.label: March on them

do.remember: marched to put the boundary stone back by force

options.result: The stone goes back, and a few of theirs come home bleeding. They will remember.

options.label: Swear an oath before the gods
options.result: Both sides swear by the gods at a new stone, carved with the oath. The fields are quiet, for now.

options.label: Let them have the field
options.result: The field is lost. Some call it wisdom, some cowardice.

events.title: A Tomb for a Great One
events.source: The Royal Tombs of Ur held lyres, gold, lapis and the Standard of Ur
events.text: One of our greatest has died. The elders say a great one should go below with music and gold, as the old kings did.

options.label: Bury them with treasures
options.result: A lyre with a bull's head is laid in the tomb. People speak of the burial for years.

options.label: Keep the treasures for the living
options.result: The dead one goes below in a reed mat, as the poor do.

tales.name: The Flood and the Boat
tales.source: The Eridu Genesis; Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh
tales.text: The gods decided to drown the noisy people. But wise Enki whispered to a reed wall, so that the good man behind it would hear: tear down your house, build a boat. For seven days and nights the flood swept the land. Then the boat came to rest on a mountain, and the man sent out a dove, a swallow and a raven.
tales.moral: the wise prepare before the water rises

tales.name: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta
tales.source: Sumerian epic poem, copied c. 1800 BCE
tales.text: The king of Uruk sent his messenger over seven mountains to Aratta again and again, until the message grew too long to remember. So the king patted some clay and set words on it like a tablet. Before that day, the poem says, no one had ever put words on clay.

tales.name: Inanna Carries the Gifts to Uruk
tales.text: Inanna went to drink with Enki in Eridu. Merry with beer, he gave her the gifts of the gods: kingship, the arts of the scribe, the craft of the smith, music, wisdom. When he woke he wanted them back, but Inanna had already sailed home to Uruk with her boat full.
tales.moral: a city is made of many gifts

tales.name: The Hymn to Ninkasi
tales.text: Ninkasi, you are the one who handles the dough with a big shovel, who soaks the malt in a jar, who spreads the cooked mash on reed mats. When you pour out the beer, it is like the rush of the Tigris and the Euphrates.
